notes: Hindu Kampili fell to Muhammad ibn Tughluq's army in 1327; Sangama brothers taken to Delhi. Tughluq sultans stayed Muslim, Persian the court language, and pursued direct control of southern Hindu powers; no adoption of Hinduism.

source1: M. A. Dandamayev, 'Cyrus iii. Cyrus II the Great', Encyclopaedia Iranica - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/cyrus-iii
notes: Cyrus took Babylon 539 BCE, claimed Marduk chose him, restored Esagila and returned cult statues (Cyrus Cylinder, Babylonian script), as pragmatic patronage while Achaemenids kept Ahura Mazda worship (Cyrus's Zoroastrianism debated).

source1: A. D. H. Bivar, 'Hephthalites', Encyclopaedia Iranica - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/hephthalites
source2: A. Mokeev, K. Belek, N. Abdimitalip Uulu, 'Influence and Traces of Buddhism on Traditional Beliefs of the Kyrgyz People', Belleten 89(314), 2025 - https://belleten.gov.tr/eng/full-text/3782/eng
notes: Turks and Sasanians crushed Hephthalites c. 560; realm religiously mixed (Buddhist sites, Brahmanical art). Taspar Qaghan (r. 572-581) founded a sangha per the Sogdian-script Bugut inscription, but Buddhism never became lasting Turk court religion.

source1: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'The Empires of the Western Sudan: Songhai Empire', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, 2000 - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/sghi/hd_sghi.htm
notes: Askia Songhai actively promoted Islam; Timbuktu and Jenne were centers of Islamic learning. Conquerors were the Saadi sharifian dynasty of Morocco (al-Mansur), whose expedition took Gao, Timbuktu and Jenne in 1591. Both Muslim, Arabic-literate.

source2: M. Hill and J. P. Allen, 'Egypt in the Third Intermediate Period (ca. 1070-664 B.C.)', Metropolitan Museum Heilbrunn Timeline, 2004 rev. 2018 - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/tipd/hd_tipd.htm
notes: Kush emerged from an Egyptianized population; Amun-Re cult strongly entrenched among Kushites. Piye opened his campaign with a ritual visit to Thebes and left a great victory stela; the 25th Dynasty saw itself restoring true Egyptian traditions.

source1: National Palace Museum (Taipei), 'Religious Tolerance', Chengde Summer Resort exhibition - https://theme.npm.edu.tw/exh111/ChengdeSummerResort/en/page-4-2.html
source2: Hongxing Zhang, review of P. A. Berger, Empire of Emptiness: Buddhist Art and Political Authority in Qing China, caa.reviews - https://m.caareviews.org/reviews/601
notes: Zunghars were Gelug Buddhists. Qing court long patronized Tibetan Buddhism (Qianlong's guru Rolpai Dorje); NPM calls Gelug the shared orthodoxy of Manchus, Mongols and Tibetans. Coded same, though Confucian state rites and Manchu shamanism coexisted.

source1: M. Van De Mieroop, 'Gutians', Encyclopaedia Iranica - https://iranicaonline.org/articles/gutians
source2: D. R. Frayne, RIME 2: Sargonic and Gutian Periods (University of Toronto Press, 1993), E2.2.1.2 Erridu-pizir, via CDLI P462081 - https://cdli.earth/artifacts/462081
notes: Gutian religion barely known (one god attested). Erridu-pizir, king of Gutium and the four quarters, wrote in Akkadian, dedicated a statue to Enlil, invoked Ishtar and Ninhursag alongside the god of Gutium. Gutian role in Akkad's fall uncertain.

source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kong' (Cote d'Ivoire, precolonial kingdoms) - https://www.britannica.com/place/Kong

notes: Kong, ruled by the Dyula Wattara and a famed center of Muslim scholarship, was destroyed in 1897 by Samory Toure while creating a Muslim empire. Dyula all Muslim, warrior lineages less strict; Senufo hinterland largely non-Muslim.

Ayutthaya fell to Konbaung Burma (Hsinbyushin) in April 1767; Taksin expelled the Burmese, ruled from Thon Buri and claimed progress toward buddhahood. Theravada prevalent in both Myanmar (dominant since 11th century) and Thailand; literate courts.

source2: J. Hettiarachchy, Buddhism in the Northern Deccan under the Satavahana Rulers, PhD thesis, SOAS University of London, 1973 - https://soas-repository.worktribe.com/OutputFile/402921
notes: Kanvas were Brahmans; Puranas say Simuka ended them c. 28 BCE. Magadha population mixed. Satavahanas performed asvamedha and rajasuya (Naneghat) yet patronized Buddhism: Kanha's Nasik cave (late 1st c. BCE), later royal grants. Brahmi-Prakrit inscriptions.
